date_label: First mention in the letters 25 February 1898, already on meeting terms ('We met by chance this morning'); the concentrated run of affectionate references falls 3-9 March 1898; the association lasted to Wilde's death - Gilbert attended the sickroom, took the deathbed photograph at Ross's request, and walked in the funeral procession, 30 November 1900.
summary: Maurice Gilbert, a young soldier of the marine infantry with an English father and a French mother, was part of Wilde's Paris household of the exile years. Through the spring of 1898 Wilde's letters to his publisher Leonard Smithers report him as a daily fixture - a nightly bezique opponent whose running score Wilde keeps for Smithers, a dinner companion at a two-franc restaurant, the man who takes the cheque to the bank and writes out the signatures Wilde is too tired to write - in a register that keeps sliding from domestic to amorous: Gilbert's 'beaux yeux', a heart 'unfortunately lost' on a side-bet, a friend who 'grows dearer to me daily' and is 'sweeter than ever'. The editors' own note calls him one of Wilde's closest and most devoted friends of the last years, and he was present through the final illness, took the deathbed photograph and walked behind the hearse in November 1900.

sources.quote: Maurice took it to the bank, so I dare say it was on account of his beaux yeux. He grows dearer to me daily, and we now dine at a restaurant for two francs!
sources.context: Wilde to Leonard Smithers, Saturday [postmark 5 March 1898], on café paper, Paris; the 'it' is Smithers's cheque, which 'with reckless confidence, the banker cashed'. 'beaux yeux' italic in the original. The same letter ends: 'Maurice says he is too old to play marbles, and I am too young to begin, so we bezique our youthful lives away.'
sources.supports: Wilde's plainest first-person statement of the attachment - 'He grows dearer to me daily' - set in the daily domestic texture (the bank errand, the two-franc dinners)
sources.provenance: PDF page 1077, printed folio 1031 confirmed on the rendered page.

sources.quote: Maurice Gilbert, one of Wilde's closest and most devoted friends during these last years. Except that his father was English and his mother French, and that he was a young soldier in the marine infantry, nothing is known of him.
sources.context: Holland & Hart-Davis, main-particulars footnote (n. 4) on the first appearance of 'Maurice' in the text, keyed to Wilde to Leonard Smithers, [postmark 25 February 1898].
sources.supports: Gilbert's identity and the editors' own characterization of the friendship; the sum of what the editors say is knowable about him
sources.provenance: PDF page 1071, printed folio 1025 confirmed on the rendered page. Whole footnote, both sentences.

sources.quote: Maurice and I are exactly quits now – twenty-six games each – but I have unfortunately lost my heart, which I carefully staked on a separate game.
sources.context: Wilde to Leonard Smithers, [postmark 4 March 1898], Hôtel de Nice, Paris; the sentence closes the letter, which runs over the printed 1030/1031 page break, and the running bezique score is a standing joke in the sequence (the previous day: 'as he has youth, and I have only genius, it is only natural that he should beat me').
sources.supports: The amorous turn inside the comic bezique register - Wilde's own 'lost my heart', staked on a side-game
sources.provenance: PDF page 1077, printed folio 1031 confirmed on the rendered page; the letter opens on printed 1030 (PDF 1076, folio confirmed). En-dashes as printed.

sources.quote: Without my morning letter from you life would be dreadful – is dreadful – except for Maurice, who is sweeter than ever.
sources.context: Wilde to Leonard Smithers, Wednesday [postmark 9 March 1898], Paris; opening sentence of the letter. The preceding day's letter (printed 1034, same page) reports 'Maurice is quite well. I am now two games behind. I wish you could make him your agent here at a salary of £400 a year.'
sources.supports: Gilbert as the single exemption from Wilde's misery in this stretch - 'sweeter than ever'
sources.provenance: PDF page 1080, printed folio 1034 confirmed on the rendered page. En-dashes as printed.

sources.quote: My dear Maurice, Bosie and I are at Nogent. Do come down either tonight or tomorrow early. I have taught them how to make oeufs à l'aurore. Ever yours O.
sources.context: Petit Bleu, Wilde to Maurice Gilbert, [Postmark 18 June 1898], [Nogent-sur-Marne]
sources.supports: The General Index lead, now read. It widens the affectionate run by a note rather than changing its character: Gilbert summoned to join a household Wilde is already sharing with Douglas, in the domestic register of who is cooking. Nothing here strengthens a romantic reading.
sources.provenance: PDF p. 1130 rendered and; folio 1084 printed at the foot. 'early' and 'oeufs à l'aurore' are italic in the printing.

sources.quote: My dear Robbie, No cheque this morning, but instead my sweet Maurice, our sweet Maurice, looking quite charming and as delightful as ever. He seemed a little tired, but of course that was the journey. He was full of affectionate memories of you and Reggie, and is quite devoted to you both.
sources.context: Wilde to Robert Ross, 24 [actually 25] May 1898, from Paris. Read while clearing the pointer that named this page for its editorial footnote. Worth noting for the shape of this relationship: Gilbert is 'my sweet Maurice' and 'our sweet Maurice' in the same breath - the affection is real and is also shared openly with Ross and Turner, which is why this edge does not read as exclusive. The same page carries Wilde joking that he means to write a novel called The Boy-Snatcher of Clements Inn, Clements Inn being where Gilbert had been lodging with Reggie Turner.
sources.supports: Wilde's own register about Gilbert in a letter to a third party - affectionate, possessive and communal at once.
sources.provenance: PDF p. 1119 read as a rendered page image; printed folio 1073 confirmed at the foot of the image (offset +46 in this region, consistent with the works.json warning that it is not constant).
sources.speaker: Oscar Wilde

null_findings.finding: POINTER CLEARED, and its own prediction confirmed: neither of the two remaining Index mentions bears on the character of this relationship. Printed p. 1073 n. 2 reads in full: 'See p.878. Reggie Turner lived at 2 Clements Inn, where Maurice Gilbert had been staying with him.' Printed p. 1222 is Ross's post-mortem account of the funeral: Gilbert took an unsuccessful photograph of Wilde dead, walked in the procession, and is one of fourteen named senders of wreaths. Both read at rendered pages 2026-08-04 (PDF 1119 and 1267; printed folios confirmed on the images). One quotation was taken from p. 1073 for its register, not because the pointer required it.
